response.query: How will we implement staggered-DiD estimators (Sun & Abraham; Callaway & Sant’Anna) to estimate group-time average treatment effects and report dynamic effects within our three-wave panel?
response.answer: Implement staggered-DiD estimators using csdid in Stata to estimate group-time average treatment effects and report dynamic effects in a three-wave panel. Focus on Callaway & Sant’Anna’s approach for aggregated treatment effects.

results.content: Two-Way Fixed Effects and Differences-in-Differences with Heterogeneous Treatment Effects: A Survey Clément de Chaisemartin and Xavier D'Haultfoeuille NBER Working Paper No. 29691 January 2022 JEL No. C21,C23 ABSTRACT Linear regressions with period and group fixed effects are widely used to estimate policies' effects: 26 of the 100 most cited papers published by the American Economic Review from 2015 to 2019 estimate such regressions. Thus, DIDe,ℓ,1,2 is similar to the DID estimator in Equation (1), and under parallel trends it is unbiased for the treatment effect in group e at period 2: E [DIDe,ℓ,1,2] = E [TEe,2] . This extends beyond this simple example: Theorem S2 of the Web Appendix of de Chaisemartin and D’Haultfœuille (2020) and Equation (16) of Goodman-Bacon (2021) show that in staggered adoption designs with a binary treatment, b βfe estimates a convex combination of effects, if the treatment effect does not change over time but may still vary across groups. We re-strict our attention to estimators relying on parallel trends assumptions, like TWFE regressions, but that do not restrict treatment effect heterogeneity between groups and over time, unlike TWFE regressions. It is therefore similar to the DID estimator in Equation (1), and it is unbiased for the treatment effect of the switching-in groups at period t, under a parallel trends assumption on the untreated outcome Yg,t(0). To estimate, say, TEc,c, the treatment effect at time c of the cohort that started receiving the treatment at c, they propose to compare c’s outcome evolution from c −1 to c to the same outcome evolution 15 among all never-treated groups n, assuming for now that such groups exist. Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) also propose estimators of more aggregated treatment effects, such as the average effect of having been treated for ℓ+1 periods across all groups reaching that treatment horizon, or the average treatment effect across all treated units that do not belong to a group treated throughout the panel. results.title: GitHub - IanHo2019/DID_Handbook: This repository summarizes the traditional and recently proposed estimators in the difference-in-differences research design.
results.content: Specifically, if treatment effects vary across time (i.e., $\beta\_k$ changes with period $k$), then the estimator in a static TWFE model will be biased, but the estimator in a dynamic TWFE model is still valid if $\beta\_k$ doesn't change across treated groups. They name this parameter as "**group-time average treatment effect**", denoted by $ATT(g,t)$, and propose three different types of DID estimators to estimate it:. Besides, as in many applications, I care more about the heterogeneous effects at different points in time but not across different groups (instead of the group-time average treatment effect defined by Callaway & Sant'Anna, 2021); therefore, I use the `csdid_estat` to produce the aggregated estimates only at periods from -3 to 4. By contrast, the first-difference placebo estimators are DIDs across consecutive time periods; if `firstdiff_placebo` is added here, the graph produced to illustrate dynamic treatment effects will be meaningless (i.e., not comparable).
